posts.title: Why Benchmarking AI/BI Genies Isn't Enough
posts.excerpt: Benchmark scores don't build trust in production AI. A well-defined semantic layer does.
posts.body:
Everyone loves AI benchmark scores. But in the real world, an AI tool being right 85% of the time doesn't cut it.

If an executive asks for quarterly revenue, they need a 100% accurate, unambiguous answer immediately. One bad number burns trust fast.

## The Problem Isn't the Model

When tools like Databricks AI/BI Genie struggle, the reflex is to blame the LLM or tweak prompts. But raw model intelligence isn't the bottleneck.

The real fix happens before the AI generates an answer. It comes down to a well-defined semantic layer.

## Data Engineering Over Model Hype

An AI agent is only as smart as the schema it sits on. A strong semantic layer gives the model hard guardrails:

- Standardized business logic (defining "churn," "revenue," or "margin")
- Clean table relationships to stop bad joins and double counting
- Clear contextual metadata

***Benchmarks have their place, but solid data engineering is what makes conversational AI trustworthy.***

A business user asks for a simple metric: the average price of a product over time.

To a data engineer, that sounds like a basic SQL query. In production, the gap between what a user asks for and how a pipeline behaves can cause silent, costly mistakes.

## The Flaw in the Pipeline

Consider a real case where a team needed to track a rolling average price. The query logic was simple and worked fine under normal conditions.

Then a live data feed cut off unexpectedly.

Because the pipeline was not built to handle missing time-series records, the calculation flat-lined. It held the last known prices steady instead of dropping the missing periods or flagging an issue.

The result was an average price that stayed unnaturally high.

## The Risk of Wrong Assumptions

To the database, the query was valid. To the user, it was completely misleading.

Anyone looking at that dashboard would assume prices were holding firm. In reality, data had stopped flowing. The user was imputing market stability from a silent pipeline failure.

## Bridging the Context Gap

Data engineering is not just about transforming tables. It requires understanding how data is used in the real world.

- Define explicit failure modes so missing feeds do not hide behind stale values.
- Match the math to the business intent instead of relying on default row counts.
- Make pipeline health visible at the semantic layer before bad data reaches a dashboard.

***A query can be syntactically correct and still tell the wrong story. Data quality depends on building business context directly into your pipeline architecture.***
posts.title: When "Average" Doesn't Mean What Data Engineers Think
posts.excerpt: Business users and data engineers often speak different languages. A simple metric like "average price" can silently break when real-world data pipelines fail.

posts.title: The Unforgiving Reality of User Trust in Data & AI
posts.excerpt: Users rarely grant second chances when an AI model or data pipeline gives a bad answer. Here are five non-negotiable rules for maintaining trust in production.
posts.body:
Building data platforms and AI systems comes with a hard truth: users have zero patience for wrong answers.

If an AI agent gives an executive a hallucinated figure or a dashboard displays stale data during a key meeting, trust is burned instantly. Even if users give the system another shot, every future output will be viewed with skepticism.

To keep a data platform or AI tool trustworthy in production, five principles are non-negotiable.

1. **Keep Your Pipelines Live and Fresh**

Outdated data is useless data. If a feed freezes or a job fails silently, the downstream metric becomes worse than an error, it becomes a distraction. Build explicit observability into your pipelines so stale data triggers alerts immediately, rather than waiting for a user to notice.

2. **Guard the Metadata Like It Is Sacred**

Your metadata layer, whether it is Unity Catalog, Microsoft Purview, or a custom semantic engine, is your temple. If table definitions are messy, access controls are loose, or schemas are unconstrained, your AI models will make bad assumptions. Strict metadata governance is the foundation of reliable answers.

3. **Strict Separation of Environments**

Production is not a playground. Testing or experimenting directly in production environments leads to unexpected downtime and corrupted data. Keep development, testing, and production strictly isolated so breakages happen where users cannot see them.

4. **Fail Gracefully Instead of Guessing**

Users prefer an explicit "Data unavailable" message over a confident wrong answer. When confidence is low or schema boundaries are ambiguous, the system should flag the limitation clearly rather than guessing.

5. **Continuously Seek and Act on User Feedback**

User feedback is the ground truth of your system's value. Establish direct feedback channels within the user workflow, such as inline rating or explicit error reporting. Active feedback collection reveals edge cases before they turn into widespread user abandonment.

***Building user trust takes months of consistent delivery, but losing it takes seconds. Treat your metadata, pipelines, and environments as production critical infrastructure from day one.***

posts.title: Stop Buying AI Agents Until You Map Them to These 4 Business Outcomes
posts.excerpt: Enterprise AI creates value only when aligned with real operational friction. Here is how executive leaders should categorize agent architectures across enterprise data platforms.
posts.body:
Enterprise AI initiatives frequently fail when tech stack architecture takes priority over business utility. To deliver real operational ROI, leadership must evaluate AI agents based on the specific organizational problems they resolve.

Across modern enterprise data architecture, agents align to four primary operational functions.

## 1. Executive & Operational Decision Support

**The Problem:** Decision-makers require immediate, accurate performance metrics without initiating a multi-day reporting request with data teams.

**The Solution:** Governed Conversational Analytics.

**How It Works:** Leadership queries enterprise data using plain language. The agent translates business intent into precise queries governed by strict semantic models, delivering immediate answers while maintaining single-source-of-truth accuracy.

**Examples:** Databricks AI/BI Genie, Microsoft Fabric Data Agents, Snowflake Cortex Analyst.

## 2. Engineering Productivity & Pipeline Optimization

**The Problem:** Core data and development teams expend high-value capacity on manual code maintenance, query optimization, and pipeline troubleshooting.

**The Solution:** Embedded Workspace Co-Pilots.

**How It Works:** Technical assistants operate directly within the engineering environment, generating boilerplate code, optimizing performance, and resolving execution errors inline to accelerate delivery cycles.

**Examples:** Databricks Assistant / Genie Code, Microsoft Copilot in Fabric Notebooks, Snowflake Copilot.

## 3. Unstructured Knowledge Retrieval & Compliance

**The Problem:** Enterprise knowledge, governance policies, and critical vendor contracts remain locked in unstructured documents, creating search friction and operational risk.

**The Solution:** Enterprise RAG Knowledge Agents.

**How It Works:** Unstructured documents are indexed within the data platform's security boundary, allowing staff to query enterprise knowledge bases conversationally and receive grounded, verifiable answers with exact source attribution.

**Examples:** Databricks Mosaic AI Vector Search Agents, Microsoft Azure AI Search with Copilot Studio, Snowflake Cortex Search.

## 4. Autonomous Process Execution & Workflow Automation

**The Problem:** Complex operational workflows require multi-step analysis, rule validation, and execution across disparate systems, exceeding the capability of static reporting.

**The Solution:** Custom Compound Agents with Governance Guardrails.

**How It Works:** Autonomous agents evaluate enterprise inputs, apply business logic, and trigger pre-approved system functions to execute end-to-end tasks safely within strictly configured policy boundaries.

**Examples:** Databricks Mosaic AI Agent Framework, Microsoft Copilot Studio / AutoGen, Snowflake Cortex Custom Functions.

***Ask "Which operational bottleneck are we removing?"***

***Matching the user's specific friction point to the right agent category is the difference between an unused AI demo and a production asset.***

posts.title: Stop Using One AI Model for Everything: Pick the Right Tool for the Job
posts.excerpt: Every AI model is built with distinct physical trade-offs. Here is why you must match model specialization to the right task to build fast, cheap production systems.
posts.body:
If you want to know why so many AI prototypes get sluggish and expensive in production, it comes down to a simple mistake: people treat large language models like identical commodities. They pick one model and force it to handle every single job across the company.

Nature does not work that way, and neither do algorithms. You would not use a sledgehammer to drive a finishing nail. Different models are built with different physical trade-offs.

Some models are engineered for strict logic and structural code. They excel at writing complex scripts, but sound rigid when you ask them for creative narrative. Other models are designed with massive memory windows to swallow entire codebases or multi-hour video streams without forgetting details. Others are built to be fast, lightweight generalists that excel at routing conversations and making API calls.

In practice, building a production system means building a toolbox. You assign a specialized coding model to write your technical logic, a fast and cheap model to extract data, and a heavy reasoning model to orchestrate the final decisions. You optimize for both speed and cost by keeping simple tasks away from expensive compute, and you abstract your model layer so you can swap parts as better engines come along.

***Ask yourself "Which specific job are we trying to do?"***

***Matching the user's specific friction point to the right model specialization is the difference between an expensive demo and a lean production asset.***

posts.title: Take Ownership of Your AI Capability—You Know Your Data Better Than Anyone Else
posts.excerpt: External vendors cannot match the deep context of your internal data. Here is why investing in inhouse AI capability is simpler and more valuable than you think.
posts.body:
Every organization operates under a unique set of forces. Beyond standard competitive moves and regulatory compliance, your business faces distinct customer expectations, supply chain constraints, economic pressures and operational quirks that belong strictly to you.

Because of this the data that actually drives outcomes for your business, the signals that determine resource allocation, pricing and risk is uniquely yours. Extracting meaningful patterns from that specific data is where your true competitive advantage lies.

When it comes to building AI capabilities around this data you essentially face two paths: outsource the build to an external partner or develop the capability internally.

The reality of outsourcing is straightforward: no external partner will ever understand your data, your business logic or your operational nuances as deeply as your own team. A generic model or an off the shelf implementation delivered by a third party will rarely match the precision of something built with real internal context. Beyond that, relying on external delivery means paying a continuous premium for domain knowledge you already own.

The more effective approach is to take ownership of the capability yourself.

AI technology scales fast, and the landscape evolves every single day. By investing directly in your internal capability rather than repeatedly outsourcing project after project, you retain the intellectual property, build long term enterprise value and create a system that grows alongside your business.

## The Actual Head Start

***Taking ownership can feel daunting at first, but it's more manageable than it looks. It doesn't require inventing new computer science, it requires a clear roadmap and calm, consistent execution.***

***You already understand your business, your market and your data better than anyone else. That's the actual head start.***

posts.title: Why Unified Governance Is the Real Foundation of Enterprise AI
posts.body:
Imagine hiring a world-class chef to run a busy kitchen, but every station marks their ingredients differently.

The prep cook labels salt as "Seasoning A," the pastry chef labels sugar as "Seasoning A," and the fridge has three different unlabeled jugs of milk, one fresh, one sour and one meant for cleaning.

No matter how brilliant the chef is, the minute dinner service starts, dishes will be ruined. Not because the chef can't cook, but because the kitchen has no shared labels, no quality control and no basic order.

Deploying enterprise AI on fragmented data is the exact same thing.

An AI model is just an exceptionally fast chef. It takes whatever raw context you give it and cooks up an answer. If your departments use separate data silos, conflicting definitions for basic metrics and adhoc privacy controls, the AI will simply blend those messy ingredients into fast, highly confident mistakes.

Even worse, without unified security, it's like leaving the medicine cabinet wide open next to the spice rack. The AI might accidentally mix confidential payroll data into a routine operational report simply because nobody established clear, consistent house rules.

Unified governance isn't about creating bureaucracy or locking all the food in a vault. It is simply organizing the kitchen so everyone operates under the same standard:

- **Clear, Uniform Labels:** A metric like "active customer" means the exact same thing in every department, so the AI never grabs sugar thinking it's salt.
- **One Security Standard:** Access rules are set once across the entire enterprise. If someone shouldn't see confidential files, the AI won't serve it to them.
- **Full Recipe Lineage:** You can trace every answer the AI produces right back to the exact source ingredient it used.

***If you want your AI to deliver real business outcomes, stop expecting it to fix a messy kitchen. Get your ingredients and labels organized first. Clean, unified governance is what turns a chaotic experiment into a Michelin-star operation.***
posts.excerpt: An AI model is like a new chef in a chaotic kitchen. If your ingredients are mislabeled, the meal will be a disaster. Here is why unified data governance comes first.

posts.title: Why Your Enterprise LLMs Need a Network Policy (Before You Deploy)
posts.excerpt: AI agents shouldn't have an open passport to the internet. Here is why network policies matter, how serverless handles it, and the risks of ungoverned compute.
posts.body:
When securing enterprise AI, most teams focus on prompt injection or data masking. But there is a glaring infrastructural risk that gets overlooked: unrestricted egress network access for the compute running your LLMs and agents.

If an AI agent running inside your environment has open access to the public internet, you are leaving the back door wide open.

*(Disclaimer: I'm a data strategist, not a cybersecurity expert, but you don't need to be a CISO to spot a bad architectural pattern.)*

## The Risks of Open Outbound Compute

Running AI agents on standard General Purpose Clusters (GPCs) with default, open internet access creates two major threat vectors:

- **Data Exfiltration:** If a malicious prompt injection succeeds, an open outbound network lets the agent quietly ship sensitive internal data to an external server.
- **Malicious Ingestion:** Unchecked outbound calls allow your agent to reach untrusted APIs or pull malicious payloads directly into your execution environment.

Giving a self-executing agent unrestricted internet access on a generic cluster is an accident waiting to happen.

## What a Network Policy Looks Like (e.g., Databricks)

Securing these workloads requires a mandatory network policy across all AI compute.

In modern data platforms like Databricks, this is precisely why serverless compute architectures and Network Connectivity Configurations (NCC) exist:

- **Strict Egress Control:** Serverless environments can be locked down using Private Link endpoints, restricting outbound traffic to explicit, approved destinations.
- **Isolated Workloads:** Serverless compute prevents agents from persisting infrastructure or exposing static IP paths that can be exploited over time.

## Consistency Is Key

A bulletproof network policy on your core warehouse means nothing if a rogue team spins up a GPC to test an LLM agent with open outbound access.

Your network policy must be enforced globally across the entire organization. Every workspace, team, and execution environment running internal LLMs must follow the exact same egress guardrails.

## The Bottom Line

AI agents are designed to take actions and call APIs autonomously. That makes them powerful, but inherently risky if left unmonitored.

***Before deploying your next agent, check the network configuration. Locking down outbound traffic with a consistent network policy isn't about slowing down innovation, it's about keeping your data inside your walls.***

posts.title: Not All Agents Are Born Equal: The High Price of Low Complexity AI
posts.excerpt: AI agents don't break budgets because tasks are simple, they break budgets because high volume ruthlessly amplifies any mismatch between task complexity and model cost.
posts.body:
When leaders plan their AI roadmap, the default instinct is almost always: "Let's start small. We'll deploy an autonomous agent to handle basic, high volume customer queries and tackle complex workflows down the line."

It feels like the safe, conservative play. But in production the compute bills tell a very different story.

The problem isn't that simple tasks are inherently bad for ROI. The problem is that high volume ruthlessly punishes any mismatch between task complexity and model cost.

## The Tale of Two Deployments

Let's look at two distinct deployment profiles:

- **The Support Desk:** A company runs thousands of agent sessions a day to answer basic customer inquiries. Every single interaction loops through tools, database queries and context history across millions of monthly sessions.
- **The Advisory Firm:** A consultancy deploys a research agent to analyze hundreds of pages of market filings, cross reference pricing datasets and draft strategic briefs.

On paper, the research agent is doing the "harder" cognitive work. But look at the margin for error in your architecture:

If you make an architectural mistake on the research agent, like passing unpruned context or over provisioning a heavy frontier model, it runs a few dozen times a day. You might waste a few dollars per run, but the output still displaces hours of senior analyst time. The value density absorbs the inefficiency.

If you make that same architectural mistake on the support desk, running an unoptimized frontier model through multi turn agent loops across millions of interactions, the compounding token burn will eat your labor savings alive before the quarter ends.

High volume simple tasks aren't unviable, they are simply unforgiving.

## Why Agent Costs Compound

An autonomous agent isn't a static, single-turn prompt. It is an execution loop.

Every time an agent checks a database, invokes an API tool, or evaluates its intermediate scratchpad, it resubmits the entire running conversation history back to the model.

When you combine that compounding context bloat with high transaction volume, simple questions become shockingly expensive if the underlying infrastructure is untuned.

## How to Protect Your Margins

To make high volume agents commercially viable, cost efficiency must be treated as a primary engineering constraint from day one:

- **Route Your Models Ruthlessly:** Match model weight strictly to task complexity. Use fast, lightweight SLMs (Small Language Models) or fine-tuned classifiers for triage, formatting and routing, reserving expensive frontier reasoning engines exclusively for high ambiguity synthesis.
- **Aggressively Prune Context:** Do not allow agents to drag full tool outputs and historical scratchpads across every loop. Summarize intermediate state and drop the noise before the next reasoning step.
- **Default to Deterministic Code:** If a step can be answered with a direct SQL lookup or standard programmatic rule, run the code. Never pay an LLM to reason through logic your database can execute in two milliseconds.

## The Takeaway

High volume workflows can deliver massive aggregate value, but they offer zero margin for lazy architecture.

***Before you scale an autonomous agent, do the unit token economics. If you run a high volume pipeline, optimize the compute down to the bare minimum, or point your heavy reasoning models where the value density can actually pay the bill.***

posts.title: The Real Data Divide: Why True Alpha Lives in the Mess
posts.excerpt: Organizations divide data into structured vs. unstructured. The real division is pristine vs. imperfect, and your biggest competitive advantages are hiding in the messy 60% no one wants to touch.
posts.body:
Most organizations look at data through a conventional technical lens: structured vs. unstructured.

In the real world of commercial strategy, that is the wrong distinction. The real divide is between perfect data and imperfect data.

Engineering teams often obsess over the perfect side of the house. We build elaborate CI/CD pipelines, enforce strict schemas, mandate zero-null constraints and map out every variable with surgical precision.

The pipelines run cleanly, the dashboards look polished and everything feels under control.

The problem? Pristine pipelines rarely contain competitive edge.

## Where True Alpha Actually Hides

If you want to know what your competitors are launching next quarter, you won't find it in a neatly partitioned Snowflake table.

If a sweeping new regulation just passed that could impact 50% of your revenue, that signal isn't sitting in a clean transactional feed.

That intelligence is buried in messy, disparate places:

- 200-page annual reports and footnotes
- Industry regulatory filings and policy briefs
- Scraped competitor press releases and job boards
- Obscure forum feedback and adhoc vendor memos

This is the 60% of enterprise context that most teams ignore simply because it is too tedious, irregular and difficult to wrangle with traditional ETL code.

Yet, that imperfect, unorganized data is precisely what makes or breaks commercial decisions.

## The Paradigm Shift: AI-First Data Engineering

Historically, data strategy was linear: clean first, transform second, analyze last. If data couldn't be normalized into rigid columns without immense manual effort, it was discarded.

Large language models completely invert that equation.

LLMs don't require a tidy schema to extract structured meaning. They can ingest chaotic, multi-page PDFs, dissect nuanced legal prose, and extract precise entity relationships faster and more consistently than manual review ever could.

We no longer need to wait for perfect data before deploying intelligence:

- **Old Paradigm:** Raw Data → Manual Scrubbing → Clean Schema → Downstream Analysis
- **New Paradigm:** Raw Messy Data → LLM Structuring & Context Extraction → Engineered Pipeline

## Building the Muscle for Imperfect Data

As data leaders and practitioners, our job isn't to wait for the world to hand us pristine feeds. Our job is to go where the gold nuggets actually live.

***The goal is no longer just perfecting the pipelines we already understand. The real competitive differentiator is building the infrastructure and ingestion capability to capture the messy, unstructured reality of your market and letting AI turn that chaos into high-conviction business decisions.***

posts.title: The VM Agent Architecture, Part 1: Running My Hobby Projects from My Phone
posts.excerpt: What happens when you put Claude inside an isolated cloud VM with strict agent hierarchies and machine-enforced governance? You can run all your hobby projects from your phone.
posts.body:
*This is Part 1 of a series on running my hobby projects with AI agents from my phone. New to VMs and Claude Remote Control? [Start with Part 0](/blog/post.html?slug=getting-started-with-a-claude-vm).*

Most enterprise discussions around AI agents focus on chatbots or RAG lookup. The real paradigm shift happens when you move from AI as an assistant to AI as an autonomous workforce inside a dedicated cloud environment.

Here is how to structure a multi-agent VM architecture where AI writes the code, reviews PRs, and monitors integrity—while you retain full executive control.

## The Three-Tier Agent Hierarchy

Never let a single AI agent write, test, and approve its own code. High-reliability autonomous operations require a strict separation of powers:

- **The Coder (Execution):** Task-specific sub-agents (e.g., Claude Sonnet) work in isolated git branches. Multiple coders run in parallel on separate issues without touching main or seeing each other's code.
- **The Overseer (Orchestration):** A high-reasoning model session (e.g., Claude Opus) breaks requirements into issues, dispatches work, and manages the execution queue.
- **The Reviewer (Governance):** A read-only model session evaluates finished branches for logic bugs, security risks, and rule compliance—including multi-viewport UI screenshots—before any code moves forward.

## Machine-Enforced Guardrails

Prompts are advisory; models can hallucinate past written rules. Safety requires hard OS-level and Git-level controls:

- **Hard PR Gates:** Git hooks physically block PR creation or pushes to main without a signed review log from the Reviewer agent.
- **Immutable Approvals:** A background service merges code only if the commit hash matches the exact diff approved by the human operator.
- **Least Privilege:** Web tools and execution scripts run under unprivileged system users with zero access to API keys or production secrets.

## Critical Lessons from Production

- **"Active" Is Not "Working":** Test functional outputs. Agents can report healthy states while trapped in idle loops doing no work.
- **Summaries Are Not Proof:** Models can write polished reports for commits they failed to apply. Always verify raw test logs and git diffs.
- **Hard Limits Are Essential:** Unconstrained memory tasks will starve system RAM and drop your remote sessions. Enforce strict resource caps on every worker.

## The Takeaway

***When agents are constrained by machine-enforced rules and monitored by secondary reviewers, your role shifts from typing code line-by-line to directing system strategy—setting priorities, approving verified diffs, and governing the platform from anywhere.***

posts.title: The VM Agent Architecture, Part 3: One Control Room for Every App
posts.excerpt: AI agents can write, test and review code around the clock. Someone still has to decide what gets built and what goes live. Here's the phone-first admin app I use to run several hobby apps at once.
posts.body:
*This is Part 3 of a series. [Start with Part 1](/blog/post.html?slug=running-a-software-business-from-a-phone-claude-vm).*

Parts 1 and 2 covered the agents and [what they really cost](/blog/post.html?slug=hidden-bills-of-an-autonomous-engineering-team). This one is about the piece I touch every day: the admin app.

Agents can write, test and review code around the clock. Something still has to decide what they work on and what reaches production. That something is me, and this admin app is how I run all my hobby apps from my phone.

## The Problem: Many Apps, One Person

I don't tinker with one app. I have several on the go, and I start new ones often just to try out ideas. Each one generates the same kinds of work: pull requests waiting for approval, issues waiting to be prioritized, messages waiting for a reply, and numbers to check.

Spread that across GitHub, a terminal, separate dashboards and a separate admin screen per app, and one person can't keep up. The bottleneck stops being the agents. It becomes my attention.

## What the Admin App Does

It's a single web app that installs on my phone like any other app, with an app switch at the top: pick one app, or "All apps" to see them side by side. Every screen follows the switch.

The day starts on the numbers and moves to the work:

- **Analytics:** how many people came, where they came from, and how far they got before dropping off, per app. Bots and my own visits are excluded, so the numbers mean something.
- **Requests:** everything sent in through the apps, with its status, searchable, and with a filter for anything still waiting on me.
- **Messages:** one inbox for everything that needs a reply or a look, sorted by topic, such as bugs or questions.
- **Approvals:** every pull request the agents have opened, each with a plain-English summary of what changed and why it's ready (or why it isn't). One tap approves it, and a background job merges it once every check is green.
- **Queue:** the issues waiting to be built, in my order. I move them up, move them down or pause them, and the Overseer picks work strictly from the top.
- **Behind the menu:** the errors visitors have hit, grouped so one bug shows once; the emails each app sends and who gets them; and the words visitors typed that didn't match anything, which tell me what to add next.

Alerts arrive as phone notifications, and staff only see what their role allows.

## The Design Rules That Make It Safe

A phone app that merges code to production is a risk if it's built carelessly. A few rules keep it honest:

- **The app holds no keys.** It records my decision and nothing more. A separate job with its own permissions does the merging, and only for the exact version I approved.
- **Approval is pinned to the change.** I approve one exact commit. If an agent pushes anything new after I tap approve, the approval no longer counts. It only carries over when the change itself is identical and just the base it sits on moved.
- **Apps stay separate.** For isolation, each app publishes a small stats export of its own. The admin app reads those exports and never reaches into another app's database.
- **Adding an app is a list entry.** New apps are set up from a standard kit and registered in one list. They appear in the switch automatically, with no new admin screens to build.

## How It Changes the Work

My job is now a few decisions, repeated: what gets built next, whether a finished change goes live, which message needs a reply, and which app deserves more attention based on its numbers. Everything else, from writing and testing to reviewing and merging, happens without me.

That also changes how I start new ideas. Because every new app plugs into the same control room on day one, trying an idea costs a few agent hours, not a new set of tools to watch.

## The Takeaway

***Autonomous agents don't remove the need for a human. They concentrate it. Give that human one place to set priorities, approve exact changes and read honest numbers across every app, and one person can run a whole set of hobby projects from a phone.***

posts.title: The VM Agent Architecture, Part 2: The Hidden Bills of an Autonomous Engineering Team
posts.excerpt: Matching models to tasks is the easy part. The real costs of running AI agents in production are the failures that look like success and the multipliers hiding outside the model bill.
posts.body:
*This is Part 2 of a series. [Start with Part 1](/blog/post.html?slug=running-a-software-business-from-a-phone-claude-vm).*

In Part 1 I described the setup: Claude inside an isolated cloud VM, with a Coder, an Overseer and a Reviewer, and machine-enforced gates between them. And I've argued before that you should [stop using one model for everything](/blog/post.html?slug=stop-using-one-ai-model-for-everything).

This post is the follow-up from running it for real. Matching models to tasks is the easy part to agree with. The hard part is the costs nobody budgets for: the failures that look like success, and the multipliers hiding outside the model bill.

## The Price Card

Here is roughly how the spend is spread across the three tiers:

- **Coders:** Sonnet and, at times, DeepSeek, about six running in parallel. This is where nearly all the tokens go, so this is where the cheaper models pay for themselves.
- **Overseer:** a single Opus session. It makes few calls, but each one steers many others, so it is worth the frontier price.
- **Reviewer:** one read-only review per finished branch. It is cheap by volume and expensive to skimp on, as the next section shows.

There's one step outside the build loop that I didn't cover last time: **discovery**. Fable is used occasionally to analyze complex domain datasets and pick out the ideas worth building at all. It costs the most per call and is called the least, because a wrong answer there wastes weeks, not tokens.

## The Cheapest Review Is the One That Returns Nothing

My earlier post warned that summaries are not proof. The review step showed a subtler version of the same problem.

A reviewer running on a budget model spent its entire output allowance on reasoning and returned an empty answer. Nothing errored. A pipeline that treats "no issues listed" as a pass would have waved that branch straight through.

The fix was a rule, not a better prompt: an answer without an explicit verdict line is not a review, and nothing is recorded. Absence of complaints is not approval. Silence is a failure state, and it should be treated as one.

## Cost Isn't Only Tokens

The bill that surprised me most wasn't the model's. An automation that kept every open pull request up to date re-ran the full CI suite after each merge, about 60 runs in one afternoon. It used up the month's CI minutes, and nothing could be tested for four days.

The agents weren't expensive. The loop around them was. Every autonomous workflow has a multiplier: tokens per turn, CI runs per merge, processes per check, reviews per day. Find the multiplier before you scale the loop, and put a hard cap on it.

## Why Cheap Models Are Safe Here

The guardrails from the last post are what make the cheap tier viable. Because the coders can't touch main, can't see secrets and can't approve their own work, a mid-tier model's mistakes stay contained to a branch that gets reviewed.

Without those permissions, you'd be forced to buy safety with model quality, and pay frontier prices for every line of code. With them, the gates do the trusting, and the models only have to be good enough.

## The Takeaway

***Picking the right model per task saves money on paper. What protects the budget in production is treating silence as failure, capping every loop's multiplier, and letting permissions, not model quality, carry the safety.***

**Next: [Part 3: One Control Room for Every App](/blog/post.html?slug=one-control-room-for-every-app)**

posts.title: The VM Agent Architecture, Part 0: Your Own Computer in the Cloud, and an AI That Works On It
posts.excerpt: Before agent hierarchies and approval gates, there's a simpler question. What is a VM, what is Claude Remote Control, and why is an AI with its own computer so different from a chat window? A plain-English starting point.
posts.body: *This is Part 0 of a series on running my hobby projects with AI agents from my phone. It's the plain-English starting point. If you already run Claude Code on a server, skip to [Part 1](/blog/post.html?slug=running-a-software-business-from-a-phone-claude-vm).* The rest of this series talks about coder agents, reviewers and approval gates. None of that makes sense until you know what the agents are actually running on, and why it matters. So let's start at the beginning. ## What Is a VM? A **virtual machine (VM)** is a computer you rent from someone else's data center. You never see it or touch it. You get an address and a key, and from then on it behaves like a computer that's always switched on and always online. It's "virtual" because one large physical server is split into many smaller, walled-off computers, and you rent one of the slices. Yours has its own memory, its own disk and its own operating system (usually Linux), and other tenants can't see into it. ## Where Do You Get One? Any cloud provider will rent you one in a few minutes: - **Simple and cheap:** DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Vultr, Linode or AWS Lightsail. A small VM costs roughly US$5–25 a month. - **Big enterprise clouds:** AWS, Google Cloud and Azure. They have the same thing with many more knobs, and are easier to overspend on. For one person running a few small apps, 2 CPUs and 4 GB of memory is plenty. Pick a data center near you, choose Ubuntu, and you're done. ## What Is Claude Code? You probably know Claude, or ChatGPT, as a chat window: you type a question and get an answer back. **Claude Code** is the same model given hands. It runs on a computer and can read files, write code, run commands, install software, test what it built and fix what broke, in a loop, until the job is done. ## What Is Remote Control? Claude Code normally runs in a terminal, the black text window developers use. That's fine at a desk and useless on a phone. **Remote Control** links the two. You start Claude Code on a computer with one command, `claude remote-control`, and that session shows up in the Claude app on your phone, or at claude.ai/code in a browser. You type into the app, and the work happens on the computer. You see every step as it goes and can approve, redirect or stop it. The connection goes outward from the computer to Anthropic, so you don't need to open ports or set up a VPN. *How the pieces connect.* ## Your Laptop Works Too You don't need a VM to try this. Install Claude Code on your own laptop, run `claude remote-control` in a project folder, and you can drive it from your phone. The catch is that it only works while your laptop is on, awake and connected. Close the lid and your session goes with it. That's where the VM earns its keep: it never sleeps, never leaves Wi-Fi and never needs charging. Set Remote Control up as a background service on the VM and Claude is always there, whether you're on a train or in bed. ## How Is This Different from ChatGPT? - **A chat window gives you advice. An agent does the work.** ChatGPT tells you how to fix a bug, and you copy and paste. Claude Code opens the file, makes the fix, runs the tests and shows you the result. - **It has a place to keep things.** Your code, notes and rules live on the VM's disk, so tomorrow's session picks up where today's left off. - **It can run things that stay up.** A website, a nightly job or a database can live on the VM permanently, not just for the length of a conversation. - **It keeps working while you're away.** You can give it a task, put your phone down and come back to finished work. ## The Basic Setup 1. **Rent a VM** with Ubuntu on it. 2. **Connect to it once** from a computer using SSH, a secure remote terminal. 3. **Install Claude Code** with one command and sign in with your Claude account. 4. **Run `claude remote-control`** and keep it running as a background service. 5. **Open the Claude app** on your phone. Your VM is now in the list. After step 5 you rarely need a laptop again. Everything else, including installing software, building apps and putting them online, can be asked for from the phone. ## What This Opens Up With a computer that's always on and an agent that can use it, you can: - **Build and host real apps:** websites, internal tools and APIs, live on the internet. - **Run things on a schedule:** data refreshes, reports and backups that happen overnight without you. - **Do research that produces files:** pull data, analyze it and leave a finished report behind. - **Run your own projects from your pocket,** which is what the rest of this series is about. It also brings real responsibility. An agent with its own computer can break things on it, run up bills and touch anything you give it access to. Most of this series is about the rules that keep that in check. ## The Takeaway ***A chat window answers questions. An AI with its own always-on computer gets work done. A rented VM costs about as much as a streaming subscription, and Remote Control puts it in your pocket. That's the foundation everything else in this series is built on.*** **Next: [Part 1: Running My Hobby Projects from My Phone](/blog/post.html?slug=running-a-software-business-from-a-phone-claude-vm)**
